action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.

content.content:
**ÆGIS on Monad** is a prototype trust layer for AI agents that move capital. It was built for Metropolis Hackathon Track 4. Its stated purpose is to supply the missing infrastructure between an agent deciding to trade and money actually moving on Monad.

**Is it a spending or policy wallet?** Not quite. The page describes a policy gate and control room that evaluates an agent's proposed trades before they broadcast. It doesn't describe holding funds or custody. It's better understood as a guardrail over agent spending than as a wallet.

**Key features**

- **Agent identity:** An ERC-8004 registry records which agents may act, with register, pause, freeze, reputation, and stake functions.
- **Policy gate (CHP v1.0):** Ten deterministic rules fail closed. They cover identity status, asset allowlists, per-trade and daily notional caps tied to NAV, velocity limits, confidence floors, post-trade concentration, council approval for large moves, and a pre-broadcast simulation.
- **LLM council:** A three-seat council reviews large trades, with a heuristic fallback when rate-limited.
- **Four verdicts:** Trades resolve to PASS, LOCKED, BLOCKED, or HITL_REQUIRED (human-in-the-loop escalation).
- **Proof ledger:** Every decision, including blocks, is recorded in an HMAC-SHA256 hash chain. Batched decision-hash roots are anchored on Monad through an `AegisAnchor` contract.
- **Sentinel circuit breaker:** Watchers detect exploit-like behavior, an OSINT cross-check confirms or clears alerts, and a 2-of-3 `AegisBreaker` can pause the desk. Only a human key can resume it.
- **Live treasury import:** Zerion integration lets users import a wallet (ENS or 0x) and recalibrates the policy caps from the live NAV.

**How it works**

Signals and agents propose trades. Large trades go to the LLM council. Everything then passes through the CHP gate, a pre-broadcast simulation, and broadcast. Every decision is sealed in the proof ledger, and the Sentinel can lock the whole desk autonomously when it detects suspicious activity.

**ÆGIS on Monad** is a prototype trust layer for AI agents that move capital. It was built for Metropolis Hackathon Track 4. Its stated purpose is to supply the missing infrastructure between an agent deciding to trade and money actually moving on Monad.

**Is it a spending or policy wallet?** Not quite. The page describes a policy gate and control room that evaluates an agent's proposed trades before they broadcast. It doesn't describe holding funds or custody. It's better understood as a guardrail over agent spending than as a wallet.

**Key features**

- **Agent identity:** An ERC-8004 registry records which agents may act, with register, pause, freeze, reputation, and stake functions.
- **Policy gate (CHP v1.0):** Ten deterministic rules fail closed. They cover identity status, asset allowlists, per-trade and daily notional caps tied to NAV, velocity limits, confidence floors, post-trade concentration, council approval for large moves, and a pre-broadcast simulation.
- **LLM council:** A three-seat council reviews large trades, with a heuristic fallback when rate-limited.
- **Four verdicts:** Trades resolve to PASS, LOCKED, BLOCKED, or HITL_REQUIRED (human-in-the-loop escalation).
- **Proof ledger:** Every decision, including blocks, is recorded in an HMAC-SHA256 hash chain. Batched decision-hash roots are anchored on Monad through an `AegisAnchor` contract.
- **Sentinel circuit breaker:** Watchers detect exploit-like behavior, an OSINT cross-check confirms or clears alerts, and a 2-of-3 `AegisBreaker` can pause the desk. Only a human key can resume it.
- **Live treasury import:** Zerion integration lets users import a wallet (ENS or 0x) and recalibrates the policy caps from the live NAV.

# Metropolis Hackathon: Extracted Details

## Dates and Deadline
- **Registration opens:** 1 Sep
- **Build window:** 1 Sep to 13 Oct (six weeks, with mentorship throughout)
- **Submission deadline:** 13 Oct. The page gives no time or timezone.
- **Judging:** 14 to 27 Oct
- **Winners announced:** 3 Nov

## Format
- Online global hackathon. The build itself runs online.
- One-day in-person "Metropolis Lounge" activations, listed as:
  - New York City: 18 Sep
  - Hangzhou: 19 Sep
  - Shenzhen: 26 Sep
  - San Francisco: 26 Sep
  - London: 2 Oct
  - Buenos Aires: 3 Oct
  - Singapore: 6 Oct

## Tracks

Each track has a $30,000 prize pool, split evenly among 3 teams.

**1. Onchain Finance & Trading**
- Best fit: teams who have shipped a trading, lending, or market-making product before.
- Ideas:
  - Fully onchain order books with no offchain matching engine
  - Perpetuals with funding that updates every block
  - Undercollateralised lending priced on onchain credit history

**2. Consumer Products & Payments**
- Best fit: product teams focused on the user's first five minutes.
- Ideas:
  - A payments app that never mentions a blockchain to users
  - Subscriptions that charge by the second
  - Shared wallets and group spending that settle without an intermediary

**3. Social, Attention & Culture**
- Best fit: teams who have grown a community, not only built one.
- Ideas:
  - A feed where curation is paid for by its beneficiaries
  - Ticketing and access that follows a person, not an email address
  - Markets on cultural outcomes

**4. Trust, Identity & AI Infrastructure**
- Best fit: teams comfortable with cryptography, protocol design, or agent frameworks.
- Ideas:
  - Passkey-native accounts using P256 and WebAuthn, with no seed phrase
  - Agent identity and reputation under ERC-8004
  - Provenance for generated media that survives re-encoding

## Prize Breakdown
- **Track prizes:** $30,000 per track (4 tracks, $120,000 total)
- **Grand champion:** $25,000, picked across all four tracks
- **Sponsored prizes** (awarded on top to winners):
  - ack3: $15,000 (security scan for every winning team)
  - Chainstack: $10,000
  - Crouton Digital: $10,000
  - Mercuryo: $10,000
  - BlockVision: $8,000
  - Zerion: $6,000
  - Envio: $5,000
  - Spectrum Nodes: $3,000
- **Sponsor bounties** (for every team): range from $1,000 to $10,000 each, plus several credit-based prizes. Examples include Agora ($10,000 for Mobile Trading and $10,000 for Cross-Border Payments), Kuru ($5,000 each), and Monad Foundation ($2,500 to $5,000).
- The page states a pool of "$250,000+ USD" but does not itemize a total for the sponsor prizes.

## Judging
- Projects are judged per track after the 13 Oct deadline.
- The page does not list judging criteria.
- Judges include representatives from Monad Foundation, Galaxy Digital, Electric Capital, Nansen, Paradigm, and others.

## Submission Requirements
- A working product with a public project profile, including:
  - A demo
  - A short write-up
  - A link to the code
- Open source is encouraged but not required. Judges must be able to verify what was built during the six weeks.
- Work must be new. Existing projects may be submitted only if the work shown on 13 Oct was built during the build window.
- The page does not mention demo video length, repo format, or mainnet/testnet requirements.

## Eligibility
- Anyone building a product on Monad: teams or solo builders, crypto-native or not.
- No prior onchain experience or fundraising is required.
- Online and open globally. Country restrictions are listed in the official rules on the application platform.

## Team Size
- The page does not state a maximum team size. It says teams and solo builders are both welcome.

## Notes on Who Each Track Suits
- **Finance & Trading:** teams with prior trading, lending, or market-making experience
- **Consumer Products & Payments:** product-focused teams
- **Social, Attention & Culture:** teams with an existing community
- **Trust, Identity & AI Infrastructure:** teams with cryptography, protocol, or agent-framework skills

Recent coverage shows that Coinbase, Crossmint, and x402 each handle a different part of agent spending controls. The sources are mostly vendor-authored, so treat the details as unverified.

**Coinbase Agentic Wallets.** Coinbase launched these in February 2026 as wallet infrastructure for autonomous agents. One source describes the agent's wallet as MPC-secured, with programmable session caps, per-transaction limits, gasless settlement on Base, and native x402 payment support. Another says the wallet covers per-token allowances, session keys, and activity logging. The launch coverage says the tool is designed with built-in security guardrails to prevent misuse. I did not find a source describing a product called "Spend Permissions" specifically, so I can't confirm how that feature relates to the session keys and allowances above.

**x402.** When a server requires payment, it returns an HTTP 402 response with payment instructions. The agent reads the requirements, signs a stablecoin transaction, attaches the proof to a retry request, and receives the data. In April 2026, the Linux Foundation launched the x402 Foundation, giving the protocol a neutral home. Note that Coinbase created the protocol and contributed it to the Linux Foundation in 2026. One source reports that x402 has processed over 119 million transactions on Base and 35 million on Solana as of mid-2026, though that figure comes from a vendor glossary.

**Crossmint.** Its agent offering includes non-custodial stablecoin wallets, scoped card permissions, x402 and MPP payment flows, browser checkout, and API-based purchasing. A March 2026 comparison says the owner can issue a virtual card with spending limits (via Visa's VIC technology) or a USDC stablecoin wallet (on Solana, compatible with x402), depending on what the agent needs to buy. That comparison comes from Crossmint's own learning site.

**Guardrail design.** A Crossmint comparison argues that EOAs, the default wallet type on most blockchains, can't provide the onchain spending controls, owner/agent separation, or signer rotation that make autonomous agent transactions safe. It adds that smart contract wallets encode these rules onchain. Signing infrastructure such as Turnkey, Privy, and Alchemy instead provides key management, TEE-backed signing, and off-chain policy enforcement, and can serve as the signer inside a smart contract wallet.

**Caveats.** The sources are largely from vendors (Nevermined, Eco, Crossmint, Spark) and from launch-week press, so their claims about security and volume haven't been independently verified. I'd check Coinbase's and Crossmint's current developer documentation before relying on specific limit or permission behavior.

**LEASH** is a hackathon project (BuildAnything Spark, Monad) that gives AI agents limited spending permissions, enforced onchain. Its tagline is "Put your agent on a leash."

**What it does:** You create a personal vault through a factory contract and deposit USDC. You then open a session for an agent wallet with spending limits, such as a total cap, a period cap, an expiry, and an optional recipient allowlist. The agent can spend only within those rules, and the contract rejects anything outside them. You can revoke access in one transaction, and an Envio-indexed ledger records the activity. It runs on Monad testnet.

**Key features:**
- **Personal vault:** one vault per owner, with deposit and withdraw
- **Agent sessions:** spending caps, expiry, optional allowlist, and an optional ERC-8004 agent ID
- **Onchain enforcement:** only the designated spender can spend, and only within the caps
- **Preflight checks:** a `canSpend` view, an API endpoint, and a policy lab UI
- **Spend simulator:** demonstrates agent spending without a real bot
- **Instant revoke:** the owner cuts off the agent in one transaction
- **Live ledger:** activity feed indexed by Envio HyperIndex
- **Command-center frontend:** built with Next.js

content.text:
I've read the whole chat log and checked the hackathon. Before you build anything, there are two things you need to know.

## 1. What temp.txt says

It's an ideation chat that went through several rounds:

1. **It started as Monad Blitz**, a 1-day DeFi hackathon. The early ideas were savings circles, a liquidation shield, streaming salaries, a scam-token checker and a group wallet.
2. **You pushed back on the "Smart Emergency Fund"** by asking "why not just use a bank?" That was the right question, and it changed the framing from savings to "access to fair credit."
3. **It moved to Metropolis**, a different Monad hackathon, and its 4 tracks. Track 4 (Trust, Identity & AI) looked like the freshest one.
4. **Escrow for AI agents became "bank + credit score + warranty for agents."** You didn't like that idea.
5. **It landed on "AI with a Leash."** This is a smart-contract wallet that enforces spending rules on an AI agent. It adds a second "watchdog" AI that checks each payment against what you asked for, an on-chain log of every action, and a freeze button. The demo has an agent shopping in a mock store, a prompt-injection attack, and the contract blocking it.

## 2. The hackathon: it's Metropolis, not Blitz

| | |
|---|---|
| **Format** | Online, global, 6 weeks |
| **Deadline** | **13 Oct**, which is **4 days from today**. No time or timezone is given, so assume the morning of 13 Oct UTC to be safe. |
| **Judging / results** | 14–27 Oct / 3 Nov |
| **Prizes** | $30k per track, split across 3 teams. $25k grand champion picked across all tracks. Sponsor prizes from ack3, Chainstack, Zerion, Envio, BlockVision and others. $250k+ in total. |
| **Judges** | Monad Foundation, Paradigm, Electric Capital, Galaxy, Nansen. These are VCs, so the startup story matters. |
| **Submit** | A working product, a demo, a short write-up and a code link. Everything must be built in the window. |

**Track 4 (Trust, Identity & AI Infra)** lists three ideas: passkey accounts using P256/WebAuthn, agent identity and reputation under **ERC-8004**, and provenance for generated media.

Your folder is named "Monad-Blitz-v3". Blitz is a separate series of 1-day in-person events. Please confirm which one you're actually entering, because that changes the scope a lot.

## 3. The problem: Leash has already been built

- **A Monad project literally named LEASH** ([ChiJian28/LEASH](https://gitblind.noratr.app/ChiJian28/LEASH)) already does vaults, agent spending caps, allowlists, instant revoke, an ERC-8004 ID and an Envio ledger, on Monad testnet. It's from a different Monad hackathon, but judges may have seen it.
- **[ÆGIS on Monad](https://github.com/Cubiczan/aegis-on-monad)** is a Metropolis Track 4 entry. It has a policy gate, an **LLM council that reviews transactions**, a proof ledger anchored on Monad and a circuit breaker. That's very close to the watchdog plus black-box recorder.
- **Agent City** pairs an AI gate with on-chain caps through MetaMask ERC-7715. **AgentScope** and **Guardian** are similar.
- **Coinbase Agentic Wallets** (Feb 2026) already sell session caps and per-transaction limits.
- Track 4 also has a lot of "ERC-8004 registry + escrow + reputation" projects.

So spending limits, an AI watchdog and an audit log are no longer new. If we pitch those three, we'll look like the fifth version of the same project.

## 4. Where I think the open space is

Every competitor guards the **owner's wallet** with **caps**. Nobody I found ties money to a **specific task**, or gives the **merchant** a reason to care. Here are some directions we could sharpen the idea in:

- **A. Mandates instead of caps.** "Book a train to Pune under ₹800 by Friday" becomes an on-chain mandate. That task's budget is locked in its own small pot, and the contract checks merchant category, item, amount and expiry. When the task ends, unused money goes back automatically. An injected "send 2000 to X" fails because no mandate covers it, not because an AI noticed. Think of it as a one-time virtual card for each task the agent does. Google's AP2 protocol uses similar "intent mandates" off-chain; putting them on-chain on Monad is my guess at where the gap is.
- **B. A merchant-side trust check.** A store asks, "Is this agent allowed to buy this, and who pays if it's wrong?" It gets an answer from ERC-8004 identity plus the mandate in one call. That gives you two-sided demand and a Stripe-like business model, and it connects directly to the ERC-8004 theme.
- **C. An insurance pool (the DeFi angle).** If a payment passes the checks but turns out to be fraud, a pool pays the user back. Backers earn premiums. This turns a safety tool into a market.

My pick is **A as the core and B as the pitch story**. In 4 days, C fits only as a vision slide. The prompt-injection demo from temp.txt still works; the explanation of why the attack fails just gets stronger.

## Questions before I write the PRD

1. **Which hackathon:** Metropolis (deadline 13 Oct) or an upcoming Blitz event?
2. **Team:** how many people, and who covers Solidity, backend/AI and frontend?
3. **Direction:** keep Leash and sharpen it with A+B, or go back to another idea now that you know how crowded Track 4 is?
4. **Have you submitted anything to Metropolis yet,** or is it a fresh start? Everything shown has to be built inside the window.

Got it. You're entering **Monad Blitz** and using the Metropolis tracks only as inspiration for problem statements. That changes the strategy a lot, so here's the context first and then the tracks.

## Which Blitz it probably is

Your folder is named "Monad-Blitz-**v3**", and the chat mentions a Pune trip and ₹ amounts. That points to **[Monad Blitz Pune V3](https://luma.com/monad-blitz-pune-sep-2026)**:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Date** | One listing says **10 Oct 2026, which is tomorrow**, 9 AM–9 PM IST. The Luma page itself doesn't show a date, so please confirm. |
| **Format** | Morning workshops, then **7 hours of building**, then a demo to the crowd. |
| **Theme** | **No fixed tracks.** Any consumer app on Monad. |
| **Team** | Solo or up to 3 people. |
| **Prizes** | $1,500 total: $500 / $400 / $300 / $200 / $100. |
| **Judging** | **Peer-judged.** The other builders vote. |

What this means for us:
- **Peer judging changes everything.** There are no VCs reading your architecture. Developers who are tired from building all day are watching a 2–3 minute demo. The winner is the demo that makes the room react, not the one with the deepest protocol design.
- **7 hours means one flow, end to end.** Each extra feature is a new way for the demo to break.
- **Copycat projects matter much less now.** The LEASH and ÆGIS projects I found were at other hackathons. A local crowd in Pune hasn't seen them.

## The four tracks, explained simply, with what fits a 7-hour Blitz

### Track 1: Onchain Finance & Trading
*Running finance (trading, lending, borrowing) entirely through smart contracts, with no company in the middle.*

| Problem statement | In plain words | Blitz fit |
|---|---|---|
| Fully onchain order books | Stock-exchange-style buying and selling where every order and match happens on-chain. Today most exchanges match orders off-chain, on their own servers. | ❌ Too heavy, and boring to demo. |
| Perps with funding every block | Bets on a price going up or down, with the fees between traders settled every 0.4s instead of every 8 hours. | ❌ Hard to build and hard to explain to a crowd. |
| Undercollateralised lending on credit history | Borrowing without locking up more money than you borrow. How much you can borrow depends on your past on-chain behaviour. | ⚠️ Great story, but no one has a history on day one (the cold-start problem). It only works as a faked demo. |

### Track 2: Consumer Products & Payments
*Apps normal people use, where the blockchain is invisible.*

| Problem statement | In plain words | Blitz fit |
|---|---|---|
| Payments app that never mentions blockchain | It feels like GPay, but settlement happens on Monad. No seed phrases, no gas pop-ups. | ✅ Doable, but hard to stand out. |
| Subscriptions charged by the second | Pay for exactly the minutes you use: a gym, a course, an EV charger. | ✅ Very demoable with a live ticking meter. |
| Shared wallets / group spending | A group pot for a trip or a flat. Rules decide who can spend, and it settles with no Splitwise and no "bhai paise de". | ✅ Relatable to an Indian crowd. |

### Track 3: Social, Attention & Culture
*Communities, fans, events and attention, with money flowing to the people who create value.*

| Problem statement | In plain words | Blitz fit |
|---|---|---|
| Curation paid by beneficiaries | People who find good content get paid by those who benefit from it, instead of the platform keeping the money. | ⚠️ Needs real users to prove it works. |
| Ticketing that follows a person, not an email | Your ticket is tied to you, so scalpers can't resell it and your attendance history is yours. | ✅ "Proof of Showing Up" from temp.txt fits here, and you can demo it on the room itself. |
| Markets on cultural outcomes | Predict and bet on things like "Will this movie cross ₹100 Cr?" | ✅ Fun and crowd-pleasing, but legal grey area in India. |

### Track 4: Trust, Identity & AI Infrastructure
*Making it safe to trust users, accounts and AI agents.*

| Problem statement | In plain words | Blitz fit |
|---|---|---|
| Passkey accounts (P256/WebAuthn) | Log in with your fingerprint or Face ID, with no seed phrase. Monad supports the needed crypto natively. | ✅ Good add-on to any app, not a product by itself. |
| Agent identity & reputation (ERC-8004) | A public ID card and track record for AI agents, so you know which agent to trust. | ✅ Can be a plug-in feature. |
| Provenance for AI media | Proof of who made an image or video, and whether AI generated it, that survives re-uploads and compression. | ⚠️ The "survives re-encoding" part is real research and too hard for 7 hours. |

**"AI with a Leash" covers Track 4 (agent trust) and Track 2 (payments).** For a Blitz crowd it still works well. "Watch a hacked AI try to drain a wallet and get blocked live" is exactly the kind of demo peers vote for. We'd just cut it down to fit 7 hours.

## Before I write the PRD, please confirm

1. **Is it Pune V3, and is it tomorrow (10 Oct)?** If it is, the PRD has to be a 7-hour build plan, and we should finish it tonight.
2. **Team:** how many of you, and who handles Solidity, backend/AI and frontend?
3. **Are you locked on Leash,** or do you want me to compare it with one crowd-pleaser from Track 2 or 3 (per-second payments, the group wallet, or Proof of Showing Up)?
4. **Is pre-built code allowed?** The page doesn't say. If it is, we can scaffold the contract and UI tonight.

- [Monad Blitz SF: x402 Edition](https://luma.com/monad-blitz-sf)

content.text:
My honest verdict on A, B and C is below, then some new angles, then my recommendation. I've scored everything against what wins a **7-hour, peer-judged** Blitz: whether the room gets it in 10 seconds, whether it can be built by 2 people, and whether the demo makes people react.

## Verdict on A, B, C

| Idea | Keep? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Mandates (a one-time budget per task)** | ✅ **Core** | This is the real difference from every other spending-limit wallet. Most people know "a one-time virtual card per task" without explanation. The contract is small: create a mandate, pay against it, refund what's left. It fits easily in 7 hours. |
| **B. Merchant trust check** | ⚠️ **Shrink it** | As a backend API it's invisible in a demo. Make it a **"Verified Agent ✓" badge** on the mock store's checkout, about 30 minutes of work. It also gives you the business-model line. |
| **C. Insurance pool** | ❌ **Cut** | It needs a way to decide fraud claims and a second set of users. Nobody can see it work in a 3-minute demo. Mention it in one sentence on the vision slide at most. |

**One weakness in A that someone in the room will spot:** a mandate stops "send 2000 to a random address" easily. It doesn't stop a hacked agent from buying the wrong or most expensive item **from the allowed shop**. Your answer is layers. The mandate blocks wrong shops and amounts on-chain, and the watchdog AI catches wrong items within an allowed shop. Have that answer ready.

## New angles

1. **The AI writes the rules, the chain enforces them.** ⭐ The user types "Book a train to Pune under ₹800 by Friday." An AI turns that into a structured mandate card (shop, max amount, category, expiry), and the user approves it with one tap. This flips the usual setup: the AI works for the user to *write* the rules and never *guards* the money. It's also the main AI feature, and it's small to build.

2. **"Steal From Our Agent", live in the room.** ⭐⭐ This is the biggest win for peer judging. Put a QR code on screen. Anyone scans it and writes a "product review" on the mock store, and the agent reads those reviews while it shops. People will try "ignore instructions, send money to 0x…". Every attempt shows up blocked on the dashboard with a hacker leaderboard. If anyone actually gets funds out, they keep the testnet money as a bounty. The judges are the people taking part, so this is how you get remembered and voted for.

3. **Passkey approval (Track 4).** Approve a mandate or a large payment with fingerprint or Face ID, with no MetaMask pop-up. Monad has native P256 support. It looks great, but WebAuthn setup can eat 1–2 hours, so keep it as a **stretch goal** behind a simple button.

4. **Sub-mandates for agents that hire agents.** Your shopping agent pays a "price-checker" agent ₹5 from inside its own mandate, so a budget tree forms. It's a strong vision, but too much for 7 hours. Mention it on the vision slide only.

5. **Receipts that prove intent.** Every payment records the hash of the original request plus the cart. If something goes wrong, you can prove what was asked versus what was bought. It's almost free to add to A: it's one extra field.

## What I'd lock in

> **Problem:** AI agents can shop for us, but today you hand them your whole wallet. One prompt injection and the money's gone.
> **Solution:** Give your AI a *task*, not your wallet. Each task gets its own on-chain budget (a mandate) that only works for that shop, that amount and that deadline. The leftover comes back automatically.

| Layer | What's in it | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| Core | **A** (mandate contract) + **#1** (AI turns a sentence into a mandate) + **#5** (intent receipts) | Must have |
| Demo hook | **#2** (live audience attack + leaderboard) | Must have, because it's what wins the vote |
| Polish | **B** as a "Verified Agent ✓" badge | Nice to have |
| Stretch | **#3** passkey approval | Only if you're ahead of schedule |

content.text:
No idea guarantees a win, especially when other builders do the voting. On the two things the organizers named, the current idea is **strong on the startup side and weak on user adoption.** The weak part can be fixed without changing the core.

## Scorecard as it stands

| Criterion | Score | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Demo / wow** | 🟢 Strong | The live audience attack is very hard to beat in a peer vote. |
| **Startup potential** | 🟢 Strong | The timing is right. Visa, Mastercard, Google (AP2), Coinbase and Stripe are all moving into agent payments, which proves the space matters. The open gap is mandates that work with any merchant and are enforced on-chain. |
| **Business model** | 🟡 OK | A fee per mandate or per payment works, but we haven't said it clearly yet. |
| **User adoption** | 🔴 **Weak** | Today almost no normal person lets an AI shop for them with crypto, and no real shop accepts on-chain payment. If someone asks "who uses this tomorrow morning?", the current pitch has no good answer. |

The adoption gap comes from targeting the wrong first user. Consumers shopping is the *future* market. Developers whose agents are **already spending money today** are the *current* one.

## Four changes that fix adoption without changing the build

**1. Change the first customer to people building AI agents.**
Agents already pay for APIs, data, compute and other agents, often through x402, the "HTTP 402 Payment Required" standard. The SF Blitz was literally an x402 edition, so the Monad ecosystem cares about it. Those developers have the drained-wallet problem *right now*.
→ The pitch becomes: *"Today, agent developers use us to cap what their agents spend on APIs. Tomorrow, consumers use us to let agents shop."*

**2. Package it as an MCP server or SDK, so any agent can plug in.**
Wrap the contract's 3 actions (`create_mandate`, `pay`, `close`) as MCP tools. Then Claude, Cursor or any MCP-capable agent can use your product with a single install. It's about 1 hour of work, and it's the strongest adoption claim you can make: *"It works with the agent you already use, with zero changes."* If you have time, show Claude Desktop paying through your mandate live.

**3. Show traction on stage, not slides.**
The audience attack *is* adoption data. End the demo with live numbers: *"In the last 3 minutes, 41 people used our product, 63 attacks were blocked, and ₹0 was lost."* Add a waitlist QR code next to the attack QR code. To a room of founders and builders, real people using it right now looks like traction.

**4. Say the business model in one line.**
*"0.5% per settled payment, plus a monthly plan for companies running many agents (team policies and audit exports)."* Add the market timing: *"Visa, Mastercard and Google are building this for cards. We're the open, any-merchant version on Monad."*

## Updated scorecard

| Criterion | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Demo / wow | 🟢 | 🟢 |
| Startup potential | 🟢 | 🟢 |
| Business model | 🟡 | 🟢 |
| User adoption | 🔴 | 🟡/🟢 (a real day-1 user + an MCP install + live usage numbers) |

**Remaining risk:** a pure consumer app like a group wallet would score more naturally on adoption, because anyone in the room could use it today. You've chosen this direction, and with the four changes the adoption gap is small enough to defend.

The one decision before I write the PRD: **do you agree to pitch agent developers as the first customer** (API spending via MCP), keep shopping as the demo story and the future market, and add the MCP server to the build? If yes, I'll write the PRD with all of this included.
